A notice inside a card carries `inline`, or WordPress's `common.js` lifts it above the tabs. `SettingsTabHeadingIconTest` holds the tab-icon half and `BoxedSectionHeadingIconTest` every other h2 the plugin prints under `includes/` and `templates/admin/`, statically; a file passes with a bare h2 only by being named there with why it is not an admin section (a core screen, the public site, an e-mail, the PDF). That guard read a fixed list of files until #1631, and a list is how the recruitment editors and the scheduling dashboard kept a bare heading — scan the tree, name the exceptions. The boxes are only visible rendered, which is how they drifted — the #1613 and #1631 audits screenshotted every screen in a throwaway WordPress to find them.
- **An area wears one icon and one name everywhere, the admin menu included** (#1640, #1641). `Core\PluginAreas` maps each plugin area to its menu item, its registry class and its translated name, and the WordPress menu, the documentation tree and Settings → Modules all read it; `PluginAreasAgreementTest` holds them together. It is its own class rather than a map inside `Icons` because it now carries names too — a name that encodes a neighbour's scope (see the opening of this file). The canonical names are the menu's: Certificates, Scheduling (its two modules Personal Calendars and Audience Calendars), Reregistration, Recruitment, Short URLs, Date Messages, FFC Settings. A module name is Title Case where it names the area (menu, headings, tabs, groups); a label describing a kind of message or option stays sentence case like its neighbours. **A path a reader is sent to — "Settings → *Tab*" — must name a tab that exists**: `SettingsPathReferenceTest` reads every translatable string, so renaming a tab fails CI until each path to it is rewritten. The menus register with the icon `'none'` and `Icons::menu_stylesheet()`, attached to core's `admin-menu` sheet on every screen, draws the registry mask in `currentColor`, so the icon takes the colour WordPress gives the item for the scheme, hover, current page and folded menu, and `LinkText` in forced colours. **Not a base64 SVG `icon_url`**: core's svg-painter recolours `fill`, and the registry draws strokes, so the icon would keep one colour whatever the scheme. A new top-level menu joins `AREAS` and registers with `'none'`.
- **A dashicon survives only where a third party supplies it.** Tab lists that a filter can extend (Scheduling settings, Recruitment, the form editor) name a registry class and go through `Icons::tab_class()`, which still draws a bare dashicon slug a third-party tab passes, so opening the list to plugins did not break when the plugin's own tabs moved. That fallback is the only dashicon left in the plugin's own markup: `DashiconsChromeOnlyTest` freezes the allowed files with an exact count and a reason each, so a file that gains one fails, and so does an allowed file that loses its last.

### Controls (one family — #1745)

A setting that picks among a few values is drawn by a control from the `ffc-control-*` family, chosen by what the values ARE, never by how they look:

| Values | Control | Helper |
| --- | --- | --- |
| two (on/off) | toggle | `AdminUI::render_toggle()` |
| an ORDERED scale of 3 to 11 | steps | `AdminUI::render_steps()` |
| 2 to 6 with no order | segmented | `AdminUI::render_segmented()` |
| anything else | a `<select>` | — |

- **One toggle, everywhere** (#1748). `.ffc-control-toggle` is the only on/off control, the user dashboard's included — it had a second implementation that hid its checkbox with `display: none`, which took it out of keyboard reach. A toggle built in JS or by hand prints the same markup `render_toggle()` does, mark class included. **The mark is the default** (#1873): a check or a cross on the knob, so on and off do not rest on colour alone; `'mark' => false` opts a toggle out, and no guard enforces it, because a toggle may go without it on purpose; the knob is white in both themes, so the mark's ink is fixed too, and the drawings come from `Core\Icons` through `--ffc-icon-mask-*` custom properties (`Icons::MASKS`).
- **Order is the test for steps.** A rail and a fill say "more of the same thing"; three unrelated choices on a rail lie about their relation. Off → Moderate → Strict is a scale; Dark / Light / Auto is not.
- **A segment's name is short; the explanation is a description.** A select hid the long option text until opened; a segmented row shows every name at once, so `On (always dark)` became `On` and the sentence moved to `descriptions`, of which only the chosen one shows (#1750).
- **Out of range is handled, not refused.** `render_steps()` or `render_segmented()` given fewer or more options than it draws prints a select, so the field still works, and calls `_doing_it_wrong()` naming the control that fits — which surfaces under `WP_DEBUG`, where the developer is.
- **Every control is native inputs plus CSS.** Radios or a checkbox carry the value, so the form posts without a script, the arrow keys and screen readers work, and autosave (`data-ffc-autosave-key` / `-form-key` on the inputs) saves the group as one field with no change to the widget.
- **Parameters for what varies, custom properties for fine tuning.** Palette, size, shape, width and which labels show are parameters that become classes; anything finer is a `--ffc-control-*` property set by a module class or inline. A palette or tone colours through tokens only and stays inside `:where()`, so a state such as disabled always wins over the colour of the chosen value.
- **One state language.** Hover and pressed draw a halo (`--ffc-control-halo`), keyboard focus the 2px primary ring, and disabled takes the colour away instead of fading — `opacity` would multiply down the contrast `DarkModeCssTest` measures.
- **The name is the family's, not the screen's or the count's** (the rule at the top of this file). The steps control began as a "three-position switch" and was renamed before it shipped because "three" stopped being true the day the limit became eleven.

### Buttons (one family — #1874)

An action is drawn by a `.ffc-btn` button whose category says what the action does, never how loud it should look. One family serves the admin and the public pages; the context comes from tokens, not from a second family.

| Category | Use | Look |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `primary` | completes the screen's work — one per screen or form | solid accent |
| `neutral` | opens, picks or navigates | soft grey ground |
| `create` | adds something | soft success ground, success text |
| `caution` | undoes or recomputes without losing data | soft warning ground, warning text |
| `danger` | deletes or empties | soft danger ground, danger text |

- **One markup, two helpers.** `Core\Button::html()` / `::render()` in PHP — `AdminUI::button()`, `render_button()` and `render_save_button()` (the settings forms' `p.submit`) are its admin entry points — and `FFC.button()` / `FFC.buttonHtml()` in `ffc-core.js`, which print the same markup. An unknown category draws `neutral` and calls `_doing_it_wrong()`; an unknown icon is dropped the same way. Both refuse an `on*` attribute, so a button that needs an inline `confirm()` is written out with the family's classes by hand, with the reason beside it.
- **Every button carries a `Core\Icons` class** on the element itself, drawn as the usual `::before` mask, so a script that rewrites the label keeps the icon. A meaning the registry lacks is proposed to the maintainer before a drawing is added ("Icons" above); until then the button takes the closest existing icon.
- **The tonal ground is the token pair the notices already use** (`--ffc-*-bg` with `--ffc-*-text`), with the tone's `-border` token on hover, so `DarkModeCssTest` measures each category in both themes. A link button restates its colour in `:hover`, `:focus` and `:active`, because core's `a:hover` outranks a single class.
- **Shape by context.** The default is the public one, 40px tall for touch, reading `--ffc-radius-sm` and inheriting the font, which is what `Core\PublicDesign` sets on `.ffc-shortcode` in the light theme. `body.wp-admin .ffc-btn` changes only the shape: 34px, the 8px corner, the panel's text size.
- **Disabled takes the colour away** (`:disabled`, `.disabled` or `aria-disabled` on a link), never fades: the theme rule below on `opacity`. Focus is the 2px `--ffc-border-focus` ring. In forced colors every category takes a `ButtonText` contour and a disabled one `GrayText`.
- **Every plugin button is in the family, the public screens and the user dashboard included** (#1874 part 2). The dashboard painted a family of its own on core's `.button` until then; its sheet keeps only layout (a compact size in a table row, the filter bar's 34px). `.ffc-btn-secondary` and `.ffc-btn-success`, the names the public screens used before the family had categories, are gone. The certificate screens joined in #1880 — the form's Submit, Verify, Download PDF, Copy and the quiz's Start again — and their old classes (`.ffc-submit-btn`, `.ffc-download-btn`, `.ffc-download-pdf-btn`, `.ffc-success-download-btn`, `.ffc-copy-btn`, `.ffc-manual-verify-btn`) stay on the markup as hooks for scripts and an install's own CSS, with no rule of ours. The public CSV screen joined in #1881 — its info screen and the open-early, extend-end and schedule-exception dialogs — and `.ffc-info-btn` is gone with no successor. Outside it on purpose: the components that are not action buttons (tabs, the calendar's month arrows).
- **The admin screens joined the family under #1904**, and no plugin markup names a WordPress button class any more — `.button*`, `page-title-action`, `submit_button()` — outside the core user screens and the `wp_die()` unsubscribe page, where WordPress's own buttons surround ours. `CoreButtonClassRatchetTest` blocks at zero ("Quality gates and testing" → "Core-button-class ratchet"). A header action is a family button too (Add New is `create` + `plus`, Export CSV `neutral` + `download`), and a settings form's save is `render_save_button()` passing the label as `value`, so the form posts what `submit_button()` posted. A meaning the registry lacked got its icon first, in the same issue.
- **On/off is a toggle, not a pair of buttons** (#1904). A list row that switches a record — a date-message rule, a short URL — draws `AdminUI::render_toggle()` with `RecordAutosave::attrs()`, which saves the moment it flips; an Activate / Deactivate button that reloaded the page was a state dressed as an action. A neutral button that picks one of a few views (the message preview's Computer / Phone) carries `aria-pressed`, and the pressed one wears the accent, from `ffc-common.css` beside the family.
- **A confirm that moves a deadline is `caution`, and its Cancel is `neutral` with `cross`** (#1881): opening a form early, postponing its close and a participant's schedule exception change what everyone else sees, so they are not the dialog's `primary`, and the defensive default is the focus on Cancel, not a louder Cancel. The confirm wears its trigger's icon.
- **Busy is a state, not a look** (#1881). A script that starts a long action sets `.ffc-btn-loading` (with `disabled`): the label stays, the cursor is `progress` and a ring in the text colour turns after the label, from `ffc-common.css` beside the family. It left `ffc-pdf-core.css`, where it hid the label behind a white spinner and faded the button.
- **Width is layout, not a category.** `.ffc-btn-block` makes a button fill its container, as the certificate form's Submit does (#1880); it carries no colour, so the category still says what the action does.
- **An icon-only button is the one exception to the visible label, never to the label** (#1879). `icon_only` / `iconOnly` adds `.ffc-btn-icon`: a square (32px public, 28px admin) with the icon centred and no text, and the label becomes its `aria-label` and `title`. Without a label or a registry icon nothing is printed (`_doing_it_wrong()` in PHP, `null` in JS). A dialog's close is `neutral` and a row's remove `danger`, both with `cross`; the screen's old class stays as the script hook, its sheet keeping only position. `IconOnlyButtonTest` refuses a `<button>` or `<a>` holding only a `&times;`, and an `.ffc-btn-icon` without an `aria-label`.
- **A button whose content is more than a label is written by hand with the family's classes**: the calendar exporter (a caret after the label) and the section pager's keys, whose digit or arrow IS the label and so carry no icon. The current page is a state, so `aria-current` paints it, never the `primary` category.
- **Public Design's error colour reaches the danger tone** — `--ffc-danger-text`, `-border` and a derived `-bg`, as the information colour does (#1842) — and only when it differs from the default, so the sheet's hand-tuned pair stays otherwise.

### Admin layout (one standard — #2486)

Every admin screen of ours is one of four shapes, and each reads the same layout tokens from `ffc-common.css` (`--ffc-admin-nav-width`, `--ffc-admin-side-width`, `--ffc-admin-gap`, `--ffc-admin-side-top`, `--ffc-admin-side-max-height`):

- **A module dashboard** opens a module that has several sections: a row of stat cards, then `.ffc-dashboard` — one `Core\AdminDashboard::section_card()` per section (icon, title, `figures()`, the buttons that open it) and an `aside.ffc-dashboard__side` with what needs a look now. A bare `?page=` opens it.
- **A section page** is a page of its own in the WordPress submenu, at the same `?page=X&tab=Y` it had as a tab, so links and bookmarks keep working; the module registers its submenus and highlights the current one through `submenu_file`. A list there uses the shared list top (`.ffc-list-filters` in a card, row actions as buttons in an Actions column).
- **An editor or a settings screen** is a vertical menu card, the open panel and a side column (`.ffc-editor`, `.ffc-settings-tabs`), the side column kept even when it is empty, so the panel has the same width on every tab.
- **A simple edit screen** is the editor without the menu: one content column, Save as the first card of the side column, Back a button beside the title.

Content takes the width left beside the menus — no `max-width` on a wrap or a card — and the vertical menu and the side column are sticky, from the top token. A box is the one `.card` (`ffc-settings-wrap` or `ffc-boxed` on the wrap), and the first card of a column starts level with the other column: a card or a row of cards never carries its own top margin there. `AdminLayoutTokensTest` holds the sheets that read the tokens; whether a screen looks right is only visible rendered, so a layout change is screenshotted before it ships.

**Four check-in screens follow their approved mockups where those depart from this standard (#2782).** The maintainer decided it, so the departures are recorded rather than re-argued. Presence terminals: the title carries a Pair terminal button, and the table sits in a card with no heading of its own, a footnote under it. Check-in settings: five sections with no intro card, saved together by one **Save changes** button instead of the settings autosave, so its keys left the autosave allowlist. An event's Check-in tab: a window card with editable *Opens* / *Closes* times, the paths card as one form, and a side column of its own (Save, attendance by path, the unsent-readings warning) shown only on that tab through `data-ffc-vtab-only`, while the day summary stays on the other tabs; who may check in and the paths left the record autosave. Presence devices: *Needs attention* is a full-width card above the device list, drawn only when something waits, instead of a side column, so the screen has no `ffc-dashboard__side`.

### Inline CSS (one rule, a short list of exceptions — #1837)

**A rule belongs in the sheet the screen enqueues, never in a `style=""`.** An inline declaration is invisible to every guard in this section, beats the tokenized class on specificity (item 6 under "Theme"), and so does not follow the dark theme. When markup — PHP or a string a script builds — needs a look, give it a class and put the rule in the sheet that loads on that screen, reading tokens; read the enqueue gate first, because a rule in a sheet the screen does not load is a style that vanished (the #1171 lesson). Moving a declaration out of `style=""` changes specificity: the class has to keep winning wherever the attribute did, so check the rules it now competes with (core's `.wrap .notice`, `input[type="color"]`, a component's `p` margin) and render the screen before and after.

What legitimately stays inline is the list `InlineStyleTest` freezes, and it is short on purpose: an **e-mail body** (Gmail and Outlook ignore sheets); a **document** html2canvas rasterises — certificate, record, receipt; a **colour an operator picked**, carried as a custom property or through `ContrastColor`; a **run-time value** (a progress width, a fitted scale, a position under a button); a **document of its own** — an iframe preview, the e-mail preview, the print window; **CSS generated on purpose** (`Icons::menu_stylesheet()`, `PublicDesign`, the recruitment badge palette); a `<style>` inside **`<noscript>`**; and the **PDF generator's own UI**, which also runs on pages that load no plugin sheet. **A static `style="display:none"` on an element a script shows stays too**: jQuery's `.show()` restores the sheet's `display` only when the hide was inline — with a class or `hidden` it writes the tag's default, `block` for a flex modal — and a theme's `[hidden] { display: none !important }` would beat it on the public site.

### Theme (one palette, one root class — #1126)

Every colour the plugin paints comes from a `var(--ffc-*)` token declared in `assets/css/ffc-common.css`. The dark theme is that same sheet's `:root.ffc-dark-mode` block redefining part of the tokens — **the dark theme is the light theme overridden, never a second set**, which is why `DarkModeCssTest::palette('dark')` merges the two before measuring. `AssetHelper::enqueue_dark_mode()` puts the class on `<html>`, reading `ffc_settings['dark_mode']` (`off` / `on` / `auto`).

**The plugin's own setting is the single source of truth. There is ZERO `prefers-color-scheme` in the CSS** — the OS is consulted inside `ffc-dark-mode.js`, and only when the setting is `auto`. A rule keyed on the media query would silently outrank the administrator's choice; don't add one.

**Seven things the #1126 arc measured that are not guessable, each of which shipped as a defect first:**

1. **The palette alone is not the theme.** A fully tokenized sheet renders light when the toggle script never reaches the page — every `var(--ffc-*)` resolves through the light block. Four public screens were in exactly that state.
2. **An undeclared custom property invalidates the WHOLE declaration.** It does not fall back to the literal that was there before, so the element renders with no colour at all. Tokenizing a sheet whose enqueue does not depend on `ffc-common` makes the screen *worse*. A local `:root { --ffc-… }` inside a component is the same defect wearing a different hat: it shadows the palette for everything inside, so `:root.ffc-dark-mode` can never reach it.
3. **Text that declares no `color` inherits from OUTSIDE this repository** — core's `body { color: #3c434a }` in wp-admin, the active theme on a public page. Both are near-black: **1,28:1** on a dark ground. The palette therefore carries a base pair per root we own (`body.wp-admin` — never bare `body`, since the class also lands on public pages).
4. **A form control does not inherit `color` at all.** `<button>`, `<input>`, `<select>` and `<textarea>` take `buttontext` / `fieldtext` from the user agent, so the base pair cannot reach them. **A rule that paints a control's ground must paint its text.**
5. **`opacity` on a row fades text and ground together**, multiplying down whatever contrast the tokens guaranteed — and the pair meter cannot see it, because the tokens stay correct. Say state with colour, not with opacity. `OpacityContrastTest` freezes every `opacity` below 1 in the sheets, per sheet and per selector, each with its reason, a ratchet both ways; it cannot read contrast (what fading does depends on what is behind the element, which is DOM, not stylesheet), so what it guarantees is that none enters without somebody having looked. Three categories are legitimate: an **inactive component** (SC 1.4.3 exempts it), a **transient state** (loading, `:hover`), and **`opacity: 0`**.

**Read the emitter for the root before believing a contrast measurement.** Measuring an element in a bare page — no `body.wp-admin`, no `.ffc-shortcode` wrapper — reproduces defect 3 perfectly, because the base pair is keyed on exactly those roots, and reports a defect the real screen does not have. A static guard cannot replace that render: many rules paint a surface token without declaring text, and nearly all are correct because their text descends from a root that is on the list. What separates a real defect from those is the computed colour under the real ancestors.

6. **An inline `style=""` beats the tokenized class.** Tokenizing is dead code while an inline colour exists. Where the background is a colour the *operator* picks, no token can work — the foreground comes from `Core\ContrastColor::on()`, which computes it by WCAG luminance. Its two candidates are pure black and white on purpose: the palette's near-black `#1d2327` drops the worst mid-tone of the RGB cube to **3,99:1**, while black holds **4,58:1** over any colour.
7. **Categorical hues are not theme colours.** The capability-group hues — one per group, and `CapabilityCatalogTest` fails a group the sheet gives none — must stay distinguishable from each other, so they stay literal with the reason inline. Same for `#adminmenu` (it follows the user's own wp-admin colour scheme), vendor brand colours, an editor theme that is dark in both themes, and print.

**Five guards, and none was written on spec** — each came from a defect that had already shipped:

| Guard | What it blocks |
| --- | --- |
| `AdminStylesheetTokensTest` A | a colour literal per sheet — a ratchet, `0` for the converted ones; counts hex, `rgb()`/`hsl()` **and the named colour** (#1168) |
| …B / B2 | a sheet reading tokens without declaring `ffc-common`; a method enqueuing the palette without the toggle |
| …C | a `var(--ffc-*)` nobody declares |
| …D | the base pair exists, paints through a token, and names only live roots; the notice's text nodes likewise |
| …E | a form control given a ground but no text colour |
| `DarkModeCssTest` | every painted pair against its WCAG floor, both themes (4.5:1 text, 3:1 signal) — **two halves**, see below |

Each carries a self-check that fails when its own scan collapses — an empty result must never read as "clean" (the #1071 / #1094 lesson).

**The contrast meter is two halves, and both stay.** `DarkModeCssTest::pairs()` is a **hand-written list of token pairs**, which measures what somebody remembered to list and is the only way to see a pair that **inheritance** creates (the base text over `--ffc-gray-100`, a label coloured by its container). The second half **derives** the pairs: every rule that declares `color` and a background *in the same rule* is measured in both themes against the 4.5:1 text floor, blocking at zero.

Three rules the derived scan holds:

1. **A named colour is a literal.** `white` is a word, so a hex/`rgb()`/`hsl()` regex misses it; direction A of `AdminStylesheetTokensTest` counts named colours, only inside a colour-valued property (`font-family: 'Whitney'` is not a literal).
2. **Unresolvable must FAIL, never skip.** A colour the scan cannot resolve (`!important`, a named colour) fails the test and asks to be taught; skipping it would pass over exactly the worst defects.
3. **Only inactive controls may sit below the floor** — they carry `cursor: not-allowed` (a full time slot, a `readonly`/`disabled` field), and SC 1.4.3 exempts text that is part of an inactive component. They sit in `DERIVED_EXCEPTIONS` with that reason, and a test fails when an exception stops matching any real pair.

**The shared skin object was measured and not built** (#1168). The tokens already deliver "change the colour in one place", so the duplicated `--ffc-X-bg` / `--ffc-X-text` pairs are syntactic, and migrating the status-badge families would need a status→skin map in PHP **and** JS, because the class is built by concatenation (`'ffc-dashboard-status-' . $status`). The guard delivers the property that mattered — a wrong pair cannot ship — without the churn.

**Standing decisions, so they are not re-litigated:**

- **Print and PDF are light by definition.** `ffc-pdf-core.css` and the certificate preview's white paper are documents that may be printed; they do not follow the theme.
- **Core screens stay light** — `profile.php`, `users.php`, the post-editor metabox. The content area of every core colour scheme is white, so our fields rendering light there is *consistent*, not a bug. Listed in `TOGGLE_NOT_NEEDED` with that reason.
- **The code editor has its own setting**, `code_editor_theme` on the General tab, immediately below Dark Mode: `dark` (default), `light`, or `auto` (follows `dark_mode`). The two sit side by side because `auto` resolves by reading `dark_mode`. One autosave key lives on one tab only: `SettingsAutosaveFieldPlacementTest` refuses a key on two tabs, because each tab's Save rebuilds its own fields and two copies drift.
- **Typography reads the scale** (#1148). Seven steps in `ffc-common.css` — `2xs` 11px · `xs` 12px · `sm` 13px · `base` 14px · `lg` 16px · `xl` 18px · `2xl` 24px — frozen by `TypographyTokensTest`, a per-sheet ratchet in the mould of the colour one. Four families legitimately keep a literal, and a fifth needs arguing: a **glyph box** sized by `font-size` (a dashicon, a `&times;`, a stat card's icon — not typography); a **hero number** a card sets deliberately above the scale; an **`em`** relative to its parent because the component is dropped into contexts of different sizes; and a value already one step below the floor inside a **phone `@media`**, where rounding up would erase the distinction the rule makes. Two sizes for one selector are almost always a deliberate `@media` step down, not drift. A value between two steps is resolved by **relationship, not rounding**: headings go up, so they keep their hierarchy, and body text goes down.
- **Each step is `max(<px floor>, <rem>)`, and the form is the point** (#1157). `rem` resolves against the DOCUMENT root, which on the frontend belongs to the site's theme: under the common `html { font-size: 62.5% }` idiom a plain `rem` scale shrinks to unreadable sizes. The px floor removes that; the `rem` half keeps the browser font-size preference these public-sector forms want. The one honest loss: under a root-shrinking theme the user's preference is absorbed by the floor until it exceeds it. **The two halves must agree at a 16px root** — `max(13px, 0.8125rem)` is an identity, not a range — and `TypographyTokensTest` checks exactly that, because a mistyped pair is plausible on both sides and only shows up rendered.
- **The public design overrides tokens, never rules, and only in the light theme** (#1677). `Core\PublicDesign` (Settings → Public Design) prints a `<style>` after `ffc-common` on public pages, through `style_loader_tag` so every enqueue site is reached. It sets `--ffc-form-width`, `--ffc-radius-sm`/`-md` and the font on `.ffc-shortcode`, and the colour tokens under `:root:not(.ffc-dark-mode) .ffc-shortcode`, so the dark palette `DarkModeCssTest` measures is never mixed with a colour picked for white. The text on the accent comes from `ContrastColor::on()`; a public component that should follow the design reads a token, not a literal.
- **A theme change repaints live.** The autosave widget announces `ffc:setting-saved` on `document`; `ffc-dark-mode.js` listens and re-applies, including dropping the OS listener when leaving `auto`. The widget must not learn which keys repaint — it states the fact, an interested script acts.

Open items and the measurements behind them are in #1148 — among them the typography scale, which already exists and is already semantic, and the trade that makes multiple themes cost more than it looks.

---

## 5. Domain conventions

### Date / time storage convention

Two categories. Pick the right one when adding a new column or touching an existing one — see #249 for the migration roadmap that retires the mixed pre-#244 patterns.

#### Category A — **Instants** (a moment in physical time)

Things like "the user submitted this form at X", "the admin called this candidate at Y", "this audit row was written at Z". Use these rules:

- **Schema**: `BIGINT UNSIGNED`.
- **Write**: store `time()` (PHP) — returns UTC unix seconds by construction, independent of `date.timezone` or the WP TZ setting. Never `current_time('mysql')`, which respects WP TZ and produces a string that drifts when the admin changes their site timezone.
- **Read**: pass straight to `DateFormatter::format_datetime($ts)` or `wp_date($fmt, $ts)`. Both apply `wp_timezone()` to render. Changing the WP TZ re-renders correctly with no data migration.
- **Compare**: ints compare directly — `WHERE ts > UNIX_TIMESTAMP(NOW())`, `BETWEEN ? AND ?`, `ORDER BY ts DESC`. No `STR_TO_DATE`, no `FROM_UNIXTIME` in the predicate.
- **PHPDoc**: `@var int Unix UTC timestamp (seconds since epoch).`

Existing examples: the Public Operator Access audit ring buffer (`entry['ts']`) was unix int from day one — that's why the only TZ bug that ever appeared there (#247) was a rendering choice (`gmdate` → `wp_date`), never a storage issue.

##### Category A exception — housekeeping timestamps

`created_at` / `updated_at` columns that are (1) MySQL auto-managed via `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` (and `ON UPDATE CURRENT_TIMESTAMP`), or (2) PHP-managed but never rendered to end users, stay as DATETIME.

Rationale: these are audit / sort columns only — they never reach a display path that would surface TZ drift. BIGINT UNSIGNED would force PHP responsibility for every INSERT/UPDATE site (MySQL cannot `DEFAULT CURRENT_TIMESTAMP` on BIGINT) with no user-facing benefit.

Current inventory (point-in-time snapshot — re-verify a column against the live schema before relying on its row here):

| Table | Pattern | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ffc_reregistration_submissions` | P1 (MySQL auto) | `ORDER BY created_at` in repository |
| `ffc_recruitment_*` | none: Category A since #2679 | every timestamp column of the module (`created_at` / `updated_at` on the seven tables that have them, the notice's `opened_at` / `closed_at`) is an instant; the list tables and the candidate edit page show them |
| `ffc_audience_*` | P1 (MySQL auto) | `ffc_audience_bookings` left this category in #2243: its `created_at` and `cancelled_at` are Category A instants |
| `ffc_short_urls` | none: Category A since #2337 | `created_at` and `updated_at` are instants (the duplicates alert and the CSV show them, the cleaner compares them); table name is `ffc_short_urls` (not `ffc_url_shortener`, which is only an option-key/meta-box id prefix) |
| `ffc_rate_limit_*` (3 tables) | P1 (MySQL auto) | — |
| `ffc_custom_fields*` (3 tables) | P1 (MySQL auto) | — |
| `ffc_self_scheduling_*` | P3 (hybrid: `created_at` auto, `updated_at` PHP) | `ffc_self_scheduling_appointments` left this category in #2679: its `created_at` and `updated_at` are Category A instants (the receipt, its PDF, the verification page, the admin list and the CSV show them) |
| `ffc_activity_log` | none: Category A since #2340 | `created_at` is an instant (the log screen, the CSV and the privacy export show it; retention and the stats compare it); existing rows were converted from the site timezone by `ActivityLogInstants`, one statement per offset stretch |

If a future feature renders one of these columns to a user, that column must be migrated to Category A storage at that point — not left as a hidden TZ-drift trap.

#### Category B — **Wall-clock** (a human commitment, no TZ semantics)

Things like "the appointment is on May 20", "the doctor sees the patient at 09:00". The value means the same thing if the user travels or the server changes TZ — converting to UTC introduces DST/ambiguity bugs.

- **Schema**: `DATE`, `TIME`, or `DATETIME` (the combined form). Stored literally, no conversion at read or write.
- **Write**: store what the user picked — `'2026-05-20'`, `'09:00:00'`.
- **Read**: render via `DateFormatter::format_date()` / `format_time()` / `format_datetime()` directly. `wp_date()` applies the site TZ when given a unix int, but with a `DATE` / `TIME` string source you feed the value as-is.
- **PHPDoc**: `@var string Wall-clock DATE in 'Y-m-d' (no timezone semantics).`

Existing examples: `appointment_date` (DATE), `start_time` / `end_time` (TIME), `date_to_assume` (DATE), `time_to_assume` (TIME).

#### Always

- Display goes through `DateFormatter::format_*()`. No `gmdate()`, no `date_i18n()`, no `wp_date()` outside the helper unless there's a documented reason (e.g. building an iCal `DTSTAMP` per RFC 5545).
- **In the browser, the same rule holds through `FFC.formatDate()` / `FFC.formatTime()`** (#2676), which read the plugin's formats from `ffcCoreConfig.dates` (`DateFormatter::script_config()`). Prefer sending the value already formatted from PHP when the server builds it; format in JS only what JS builds. Two exceptions, both deliberate: a calendar day heading writes the month by name in the WordPress locale (`FFC.formatDate( ymd, 'long' )`), and `ffc-signed-qr.js` carries its own date-token reader, because the standalone verifier inlines that file alone and cannot reach `ffc-core`.
- Filenames / log keys / API contracts that need a stable ISO format may use `gmdate('Y-m-d\TH:i:s\Z', $ts)` — but the column those filenames represent should still follow Category A or B.

### Settings reads

Read `ffc_settings` via `FreeFormCertificate\Settings\SettingsReader`, not `get_option('ffc_settings')` directly:

- Use typed accessors when one exists (`SettingsReader::emails_disabled()`, `SettingsReader::activity_log_retention_days()`, etc.).
- Fall back to `SettingsReader::get($key, $default)` for keys without a dedicated typed accessor.
- Use `SettingsReader::all()` when a caller reads 5+ keys (SMTP block, DateFormatter format catalog) and array-style access stays clearer than repeated method calls.

The debug-area toggles (the `Debug::AREA_*` constants own the list) continue to be read via `Debug::is_enabled($area)` — that helper has the canonical `function_exists('get_option')` defensive check and is the typed reader for that subset.

Classes that already encapsulate `get_option('ffc_settings')` in their own private helper (e.g. `UrlShortenerService::get_settings()`) do NOT need to migrate — they're already centralized.

### Settings writes — autosave toggles (the no-clobber invariant)

On/off **toggle switches** (`.ffc-control-toggle`, rendered via `AdminUI::render_toggle()`) auto-save on flip: mark the input `data-ffc-autosave-key="<key>"`, add the key to `SettingsAjaxEndpoint::allowlist()` (`{option, path?, type, cap}`), and have the tab call `enqueue_autosave_infra()`. This is the standard for atomic, side-effect-free boolean settings. **Two autosave endpoints exist and stay separate on purpose** (do NOT unify — bad-façade trap): `SettingsAjaxEndpoint` (`ffc_update_setting`) writes WP **options** under a global cap; `FormMetaAjaxEndpoint` (`ffc_update_form_meta`, attribute `data-ffc-autosave-form-key`) writes per-post **meta** gated on `edit_post` of that exact form. **The JS is one widget serving both** (#1116) — `FFC.Admin.autoSaveField` in `assets/js/ffc-admin-autosave.js`, wired by `bootAutoSaveFields()`, which scans **both** attributes and takes `action` / `payload` / `request` / `strings` per endpoint. The endpoints stay separate; only their client did not need to be. That statement was written here before it was true: the form-meta half was a second implementation inside `assets/js/ffc-admin.js` (delegated, `change` only, no debounce, its own badge whose CSS hardcoded hex and therefore ignored dark mode), and the cost was not theoretical — the #1114 validity guard had to be written twice to reach both halves. So a change to autosave behaviour is now one edit; **a screen that renders either attribute must enqueue `ffc-admin-autosave`** (settings tabs get it from `enqueue_autosave_infra()`, the form editor enqueues it directly), or its fields silently have no listener.

Two things the convergence measured, worth not re-deriving. Every one of the 16 form-meta fields is a checkbox from `AdminUI::render_toggle()`, so adopting the settings half's `change`+`input` binding changed nothing visible — there is no text field on that path to "save while typing", and a checkbox's two events coalesce in the debounce. And the **delegated** binding was the half *not* kept, against the original proposal: nothing exercises it (all fields of both kinds are server-rendered at page load), and adopting it would have meant rewriting the half with 115 fields, per-field debounce, multi-checkbox groups and `confirmOff` to gain that. `bootAutoSaveFields()` is idempotent and exported, so DOM inserted later has a supported answer — call it again.

**Invariant that keeps autosave and the form Save from clobbering each other — hold it whenever you add an autosave toggle:**

- The autosave toggle must ALSO be a **named field inside its tab's `<form>`**, so the form's rebuild-save writes the toggle's *current* (auto-saved) state, not a stale/absent one. An autosave-only key that a rebuild-save omits gets silently reset on the next Save.
- Tabs that share `ffc_settings` save through the central `SettingsSaveHandler`, which is **merge-based** (`$clean = get_option(...)`) and gates each section on the hidden `_ffc_tab` marker — so saving tab X only rebuilds tab X's toggles, preserving every other tab's auto-saved keys. Keep both properties (merge base + `_ffc_tab` guard) when touching that handler.
- Tabs with their own option (geolocation, rate-limit, user-access, ip-diagnostics) full-rebuild that option from their own form; every toggle in the option must be read back from `$_POST` there.

### Admin number inputs — `required`, and the three times it is wrong

Every `<input type="number">` in the admin carries `required`, enforced by `tests/Unit/RequiredNumericInputTest.php` — an unlisted one without it fails, and a listed exception that gained it (or vanished) fails too. The reason is the #1114 class: a cleared number field posts the empty string, `absint( '' )` is `0`, and what that `0` means is per-consumer and was never uniform — on the Rate Limit tab it read as "limit already reached" and barred every submission from every address; on a reregistration campaign it collapsed the reminder onto the campaign's last day. The attribute is only the cheap half: **the save handler still has to treat empty as "not supplied"**, because the browser is not the guard (`RequestInput::get_post_string( $k, '' )` then an explicit `'' === …` branch; `ArrayValue::int()` already does this, since `is_numeric( '' )` is false).

Three shapes make `required` a **bug** rather than a missing safeguard, and each is in the guard's `KNOWN_OPTIONAL` with its reason:

1. **Empty is a documented value.** The device-limit and public-CSV fields say "Inherit from global" and their save handler *deletes the meta* so the read side falls back; the audience calendar's says "Leave empty for no limit". `required` removes the only way to express it.
2. **The control is not a form field.** `ffc_qty_codes` has no `name` — it is the argument to an AJAX button. A control without a name is still a candidate for constraint validation, so `required` there blocks the surrounding form while never being submitted. Same for an empty "add a new row" line inside a shared `<form>` (`ffc_location_new[…]`, caught in #1115 before it shipped).
3. **Requiredness belongs to the field's definition.** User-defined custom fields carry `is_required`; the markup must emit the attribute from that flag, never hardcode it. Both renderers do (#1120 closed the user-profile side, where the flag had only ever drawn an asterisk). Two types stay out on purpose: a **checkbox** would have to be *ticked* to satisfy `required`, a different promise from "fill this in"; and a value posted through a **hidden** input is barred from constraint validation outright, so marking it required does nothing.

**A `required` field inside a JS-hidden block blocks the submit against a control nobody can see** — constraint validation ignores visibility, and only `disabled` bars a control (which would drop it from the POST). So the attribute travels with the block: `FFC.setRequiredWithin( $container, visible )` strips it and puts it back, using a marker attribute so a re-show never *promotes* fields that were never required. Call it wherever a block is shown or hidden — the calendar editor's four blocks, the quiz rows, and the collapsible audience sections on the user-profile screen all do. This was not hypothetical: the working-hours rows had carried `required` inside `.ffc-regular-only` since 4.1.0, so a stored row with an empty time jammed the save of any calendar switched to custom mode.

### Capability naming

All FFC capabilities follow one grammar (ratified in #488, applied plugin-wide):

```
ffc_<action>_[own_]<domain>[_<qualifier>]
```

- **Actions (closed vocabulary):** `view` (read-only) · `manage` (read-write: create/edit/delete/configure) · `export` · `import` · `edit` (modify existing records — narrower than `manage`) · `delete`. Flow-specific verbs: `book`, `cancel`, `download`, `call`, `bypass`, `submit` (create a record through an authenticated API on behalf of the public flow — `ffc_submit_forms_api`, #1861), `test` (send a sample to the operator's own address without being able to change what is sent — `ffc_test_date_messages`, `ffc_test_settings_smtp`, #1860; the matching `manage` cap allows it too), `purge` (delete by criteria, a whole calendar's past, cancelled or every record at once — `ffc_purge_appointments`, #1872; narrower than the single-record `delete`, and held only by the module's Administrator tier), `checkin` (run a booking day's attendance check-in: open and close it, project its QR, mark attendance by hand — `ffc_checkin_audiences`, #1947; on the Audience Calendars Operator tier, while the participant checking in needs no capability, only a place on the booking).
- **`own_`** marks a self-scoped end-user cap (frontend; the user's own data).
- **Domains (canonical):** `certificates`, `appointments`, `audiences`, `reregistration`, `custom_fields`, `activity_log`, `settings`, `recruitment`, `url_shortener`, `forms_api`.
- **Qualifiers:** `_pii`, `_settings`, `_reasons`, `_history`, `_smtp`, `_dangerzone`, `_presence`. `_presence` and `_terminals` name the app's presence devices and the check-in terminals inside a domain (`ffc_manage_audiences_presence`, #2743; `ffc_manage_audiences_terminals`, #2744). `_smtp` and `_dangerzone` carve the two most sensitive Settings surfaces out of the blanket `ffc_manage_settings` (#711): `ffc_manage_settings_smtp` gates the SMTP transport + Email Model save, and `ffc_manage_settings_dangerzone` gates every destructive maintenance action (delete-all, cleanups, public-access disabler, submission-link audit, migration execution). A dedicated `ffc_export_activity_log` (export tier) was also split out of the read-only `ffc_view_activity_log` so a view-only operator cannot bulk-extract the audit trail. All three ship with one-shot grant migrations that seed the new cap onto current holders, so no one loses access on upgrade.

**Settings-write auth — WP-standard, no engine (deliberate, #711).** Settings-write authorization uses the **WordPress-standard inline pattern**: native nonce funcs (`wp_verify_nonce` / `check_admin_referer` / `check_ajax_referer`) + the existing capability chokepoint `Capabilities::current_user_can_admin_or()`. Do **not** wrap this in a settings persistence/authorize "engine" — one was tried and removed as net-negative indirection (it fit none of the real writers and only hid the nonce from the WPCS sniff).

#### 3-state permission model

Every admin domain exposes a `view`/`manage` pair so each surface has three states — *hidden* / *view only* / *view and edit* — with the WP admin (`manage_options`) above all:

```
canView = current_user_can('manage_options') || view_cap || manage_cap
canEdit = current_user_can('manage_options') || manage_cap
```

A `manage` role does **not** need to also carry the `view` cap — `canView` already includes `manage`. Hidden when neither; read-only render (disabled inputs, no save, row/bulk actions hidden) when only `view`. Use `Capabilities::current_user_can_admin_or($cap)` for inline gates; menu/tab caps take the slug directly (admins hold every FFC admin cap via the activation/`ensure_admin_capabilities` grant).

#### Roles — one label pattern, four tiers (#1860)

Every module role is labelled `FFC <Module> [- <Part>] - <Tier>`, the module named as the menu names it (`Core\PluginAreas`; the Scheduling area is its two modules, Personal Calendars and Audience Calendars; FFC Settings already carries the prefix). A module whose screens split names the part in **every** one of its roles — Certificates - Submissions / Forms, Personal Calendars - Bookings / Setup — so a part's roles sort and read as one ladder. Slugs are stored values and never rename: `ffc_appointments_*` is Personal Calendars - Bookings, `ffc_calendars_*` Setup, `ffc_forms_*` Certificates - Forms, `ffc_audiences_*` Audience Calendars.

Every module has four tiers, each holding the one below it: **Viewer** (screens, personal data masked) → **Operator** (+ the day-to-day actions) → **Manager** (+ manage, export, delete, reveal PII) → **Administrator** (+ bypass and module settings where the module has them, otherwise equal to the Manager). Certificates - Forms and Personal Calendars - Setup keep Viewer and Manager only. `ffc_administrator` holds everything; `ffc_readonly` holds view caps only, never a `_pii` one. The activity log and identity resolution (`CapabilityManager::ADMINISTRATOR_ONLY_CAPABILITIES`) are `ffc_administrator`'s alone among the roles. `RoleNamingTest` holds all of it; a new module joins `PluginAreas` and ships its four roles in the same PR.

**A role only ever gains caps on its own.** `RoleRegistrar::register_module_roles()` adds what a definition grants and never removes, so taking a cap off a shipped tier — or renaming the stored label — needs a one-shot step in `CapabilityMigrator` (`migrate_role_tiers()` is the #1860 one). Beware the seeding migrations: they walk every role, so on a fresh install a role holding a seed's source receives its targets whether or not its tier owns them; `role_tier_removals()` follows those edges for exactly that reason.

#### Registry, catalog, migration

- Machine list: `CapabilityManager` (`*_CAPABILITIES` consts + `module_roles_definition()`).
- Human metadata: `CapabilityCatalog::groups()`. **Invariant** (enforced by `CapabilityCatalogTest`): `CapabilityCatalog::all_slugs()` must equal `CapabilityManager::get_all_capabilities()` as a set — adding a cap to one without the other fails CI.
- Renames ship with a one-shot, option-flagged migration that rewrites grants on every user (`user_meta`) **and** every role definition (see `CapabilityMigrator::migrate_taxonomy_renames()` + `Loader::ensure_taxonomy_renamed()`; the one-shot migrations live in `CapabilityMigrator` and role lifecycle in `RoleRegistrar` since #563 Sprint 2). Renames are a **breaking change** for external integrations referencing old slugs — call it out in the CHANGELOG.

### Security & PII conventions

A full security audit confirmed these hold plugin-wide — keep them that way (the #596 IP-hash fix was the only gap found):

- **Output escaping.** Escape every echoed value at the output point (`esc_html` / `esc_attr` / `esc_url` / `esc_textarea`, or `wp_kses_post` for rich HTML). The WPCS `EscapeOutput` gate enforces it; a `phpcs:ignore` must be justified (the value is provably pre-escaped). DB-stored data rendered on a higher-privileged screen is still untrusted — escape it (see the #564 stored-XSS).
- **SQL.** All queries go through `$wpdb->prepare()` with `%d` / `%s` / `%i` (identifiers), `esc_like()` for `LIKE`, and an allowlist (or `sanitize_sql_orderby()`) for any request-derived `ORDER BY` / column. Never interpolate request data into SQL.
- **Request entry points.** Every AJAX / REST / `admin_post` handler that mutates or exposes PII checks **both** a capability (`current_user_can` / `Capabilities::current_user_can_*` / a non-`__return_true` `permission_callback`) **and** a CSRF nonce (`check_ajax_referer` / `wp_verify_nonce` / `check_admin_referer`). Destructive actions take a narrower cap (e.g. `ffc_delete_*`). For per-user data, derive the user from `get_current_user_id()` and gate any `viewAsUserId`-style override on `manage_options` — never trust a request-supplied user/owner id (IDOR).
- **PII at rest & display.** CPF / RF / email are stored via `Encryption` (AES-256-CBC, per-record CSPRNG IV, encrypt-then-HMAC, `hash_equals` verify); searchable copies use a salted hash. Display goes through `DocumentFormatter` **masked**, for every member of staff: one shape per kind (`DocumentFormatter::mask( MASK_*, $value )`), one key-to-kind map (`kind_for_key()`, which `mask_any()`, `mask_field_value()` and `PiiExport` read), and no mask ever returns its input — a value that does not fit its shape masks as generic (#1920). A mask written anywhere else fails `MaskLiteralTest`; a value shown masked before it is decrypted takes `mask_placeholder()`. Tokens use `random_bytes` / `wp_generate_password`, never `rand`/`mt_rand`.
- **One reveal policy (#1863).** Every surface that shows, exports or mails another person's data asks `Core\PiiAccessPolicy::resolve( 'ffc_view_<module>_pii', $owner )`, which has three answers and no role list: `unmasked` is the **owner** reading their own record — what a PDF, a receipt or an e-mail the owner asks for prints; on a screen the owner asks `resolve_on_screen()` instead, whose `owner_reveal` draws the data masked behind the same Reveal with **no** activity-log row, so a shared or projected screen does not show it (#1897); `reveal` is a holder of the module's `_pii` cap or `manage_options` — masked first, then an audited Reveal (one value through `ffc_reveal_pii`, or a list page through `ffc_reveal_pii_page`, one activity-log row naming the records); `masked` is everyone else, FFC Read-only included. There is **no staff unmasked tier** any more: the module `_admin` roles and WordPress administrators reveal like the Manager does, so a new screen never draws a clear value for staff. The rest follows from that: a list draws `Core\PiiReveal::page_button()` and enqueues `PiiReveal::enqueue_assets()`; a CSV source freezes `Core\PiiExport::allowed()` in its context, masks through `PiiExport::cell()` without it and calls `PiiExport::log()` when it wrote clear values; a REST read stays masked unless the caller asks `reveal=1` and may reveal (audited); "view as user" is not the owner and reveals like staff; an e-mail to staff carries the data masked with a link to the screen. The public CSV download is the one surface that hands personal data in clear to a caller with no account: the file carries CPF, e-mail and RF behind the per-form access hash, by design, so every delivery, the batched one included, writes a `pii_exported` entry naming the form (#2341). A certificate signer's RF is the second surface that prints personal data in clear for others to read (#2582): it prints in full on the certificates that person signs, because the RF is what identifies the signer on the document. What is audited is listing them on Certificates → Signers, since that is what authorises it; the RF is read from the profile at generation time, without the `UserProfileService` full-read audit, which would write one entry per certificate. Previews, staff screens and the verification page show it masked, with the audited Reveal on the signer list. The one exception on staff screens is identity resolution, restricted to FFC Administrator, which shows what it needs unmasked; the activity log was the second until #2109, and now draws a client address and the personal values of an entry's details masked behind a Reveal through `ffc_view_activity_log_pii`, which writes no row there (#2340: each reveal would add an entry to the log being read; a type with an empty `audit_action` is not logged, and `ActivityLogActionLabelsTest::UNLOGGED_REVEAL_TYPES` names it), as the Rate Limit tab's top blocked addresses do, audited, through `ffc_view_settings_pii`. A new reveal type joins `AdminAjax::pii_reveal_configs()` (`PiiTierConsistencyTest` measures every role against every type); a new module with personal data ships its `_pii` cap on its Manager and Administrator tiers.
- **Never log raw PII.** Debug logs hash IPs / CPF — a truncated **keyed** hash, never the value — and stay behind the off-by-default debug toggles regardless. See `IpGeolocation` and `ClientIpResolver` (16 hex chars of `Encryption::keyed_hash()`) and `PreflightTelemetry` (12 of `IpAddress::fingerprint()`) (#596, #2109). A bare `hash( 'sha256', $ip )` is not a hash here: the IPv4 space is 2^32 addresses, so a table reverses it, which is what those two call sites shipped until #2109. **The truncation length is the call site's, not a plugin-wide constant**; this file used to quote one length for all of them and disagreed with `PreflightTelemetry` for as long as it did. What is plugin-wide is the rule: hash before logging.
- **Outbound HTTP.** Validate any request-derived IP/URL before `wp_remote_*` (e.g. `FILTER_FLAG_NO_PRIV_RANGE | FILTER_FLAG_NO_RES_RANGE` to block SSRF); prefer `wp_safe_redirect` for redirects.
- **User-deletion integrity is two layers over a *deliberate subset*, not every user-reference column.** The primary is the app-layer `UserCleanup` hook (`deleted_user`), which handles `user_id` on the user-owned tables: **SET NULL** (retain the row, drop the link) for `submissions` / `appointments` / `activity_log` (the last via `ActivityLogQuery::redact_user_id`), **DELETE** (purge the row) for the pure-relationship audience tables (`audience_members` / `audience_booking_users` / `audience_schedule_permissions` / `audience_form_invites` / `audience_presence_devices` / `audience_presence_requests`, the last three outside the footprint short-circuit) and `user_profiles`. `MigrationForeignKeys` adds a DB-level `user_id → wp_users` FK backstop on *those same* tables plus `audience_attendance` — `ON DELETE SET NULL` where the hook nulls, `ON DELETE CASCADE` where it deletes; its `CONSTRAINTS` map is the list — so integrity holds even if the hook is bypassed. This FK migration is **not** legacy: `dbDelta()` cannot emit FKs, so it is the sole path that creates them (absent on a fresh install until it runs), guarded by `ffc_foreign_keys_db_version`. **Beyond `user_id` (#834):** the hook also runs an **authorship sweep** (`UserCleanup::anonymize_authorship()`) that SET-NULLs the **nullable** actor-attribution columns (`submissions.edited_by`; `appointments.approved_by`/`cancelled_by`; `self_scheduling_calendars.created_by`/`updated_by`; `blocked_dates.created_by`; `audience_bookings.cancelled_by`; `reregistration_submissions.reviewed_by`; `recruitment_call.cancelled_by`; `short_urls.created_by`; `date_message_runs.created_by`; `audience_attendance.marked_by`; `audience_checkin_windows.opened_by`/`closed_by`; `audience_presence_devices.revoked_by`/`released_by`; `audience_presence_requests.decided_by`; `audience_terminals.paired_by`/`revoked_by`; `audience_terminal_pairings.created_by`) **and** the record links `recruitment_candidate.user_id`, `date_message_log.user_id` and `audience_attendance.user_id` — `UserCleanup::anonymize_authorship()`'s map is the list. The sweep runs on **every** deletion (an actor/candidate need not have data-subject footprint, so it sits *outside* the #322 footprint short-circuit that still gates the `user_id` blocks) — cost is extra unindexed UPDATEs on the cold deletion path. It is **app-layer only**: no FK backstop is added for attribution columns (they are low-risk actor refs, not primary user-owned records), and the `NOT NULL` attribution columns are left as accepted orphans (see the gaps note).
  - **The governing principle** (apply it when adding any user-linked table): *retain records, drop relationships.* A row that is a **record** (a submission, an appointment, an audit line, a reregistration) is retained and its user link anonymised — SET NULL when the column is nullable, or left as an **accepted orphan** when it is `NOT NULL` and the row is a retained/legal record (the `activity_log` precedent). A row that is a pure **relationship** (a membership, a permission grant) is deleted with the user. Both layers key **only on `user_id`** — see the gap inventory below before assuming a new column is covered.
  - **Recruitment candidate:** `ffc_recruitment_candidate.user_id` is `DEFAULT NULL` (a candidate isn't a WP user until promotion; documented in its activator). Pre-promotion there's nothing to null; **post-promotion the link is now SET NULL by the authorship sweep (#834)** — the candidacy record + its PII are retained, only the WP-user link drops.
  - **`ffc_reregistration_submissions` — accepted orphan (#822, decided).** Its `user_id` (`NOT NULL`) is covered by neither layer *on purpose*: a reregistration is a retained record, and the identifying PII lives in the `data` JSON body (partly `Encryption`-encrypted, partly plaintext), so nulling the FK alone would be a half-measure. The row is retained; the `user_id` is an accepted orphan; JOIN consumers degrade to "—". There is **no separate custom-field value table** — those values are the `data` column (and `wp_usermeta` under `ffc_%`, which WP core + the manual `PrivacyErasers` clean, but the automatic `deleted_user` hook does not).
  - **`ffc_bulk_issue_jobs.user_id` — accepted orphan (#1945).** The operator who started a bulk issue, `NOT NULL`, covered by neither layer on purpose: the job row is an audit record of counters and dates (total, issued, skipped) with no personal data, and its staged rows — the only personal data — are deleted when the job ends or expires. Deleting the operator leaves the counters attributed to an id with no account, the `activity_log` precedent; nulling it would need an `ALTER … MODIFY … DEFAULT NULL` for nothing a reader uses.
  - **`ffc_recruitment_import_jobs.user_id` and `ffc_reregistration_import_jobs.user_id` — accepted orphans (#2343).** The operator who started an import, `NOT NULL DEFAULT 0`, covered by neither layer, for the `ffc_bulk_issue_jobs` reason: a job row carries counters and dates, its staged rows are the only personal data, and the daily cleanup deletes both once the job is stale (`STAGING_JOB_TTL_SECONDS`).
  - **`ffc_identity_accepted` — accepted orphan, and the first one that is not a column (#1536).** The identity-acceptance record (#1532) is an **option**, keyed `check|field|subject`, and for `cross_store_multiple_identities` that subject is a **`user_id`**. Neither layer can reach it: the hook knows tables, and an option has no FK. It stays that way on purpose, by the governing principle above — an acceptance is a **decision record**, like an activity-log line, and the id is the identity of its key rather than a nullable column, so there is no link to drop without destroying the record. Deleting the account makes it **inert** rather than wrong: the checks read the live stores, so the finding it suppresses leaves the next scan, and the audit card's count joins in the scan's direction and stops counting it. It stays listed and withdrawable on the screen, because a row that vanishes is a suppression nobody can withdraw. **The generalisation worth keeping: the principle is about records and relationships, not about columns** — ask it of a new option or transient that keys on a user, not only of a new table.
  - **#834 resolution (was "known remaining gaps"):** (1) **attribution columns** — the *nullable* ones are now nulled by the authorship sweep above; the six `NOT NULL` ones (`audiences`/`audience_schedules`/`audience_holidays`/`audience_bookings.created_by`, `reregistrations.created_by`, `recruitment_call.created_by`) stay **accepted orphans** (a plain `SET NULL` would be rejected; they're retained-record actor refs) — nulling them would need an `ALTER … MODIFY … DEFAULT NULL` first, not worth it. (2) `recruitment_candidate.user_id` post-promotion — **now covered** (SET NULL). (3) **Row-body PII on account deletion — decided policy, not a gap:** the automatic `deleted_user` hook anonymises the *link* (`user_id` + nullable attribution) but deliberately does **not** scrub the encrypted PII columns in the row body (`*_encrypted`/`*_hash`). Account deletion ≠ an erasure request: the **manual `PrivacyErasers`** (WP GDPR eraser) is the path that additionally clears `email_encrypted`/`cpf_encrypted`/`rf_encrypted`/… so certificates/appointments stay verifiable records until a subject actually exercises erasure. The only residual is the app-layer-only nature of the attribution sweep (no FK backstop) — an accepted design choice, not a follow-up.

## 6. Legacy and tech debt

### Legacy compat shims — audit log

Inventory of the legacy compatibility shims that remain in the code by design (snapshot — re-confirm the location in code before removing; paths and lines change with every refactor, so the table cites files/methods, never line numbers). Removing them requires evidence that no production installation depends on them.

**Shim · `ffc-pdf-core.css` sections 7 and 13 — the four legacy PDF-stage classes** (`ffc-pdf-stage`, `ffc-pdf-bg-img`, `ffc-pdf-user-content`, `ffc-pdf-temp-wrapper`). *Risk if removed:* a certificate body saved before the rename renders unstyled — each has a live sibling the JS emits today (`wrapper`, `bg`, `content`, `temp-container`), so the pairs name the rename. *Why it stays:* the sheet declares section 13 "Backward compatibility", and **`git log -S` over `assets/js`, `includes` and `templates` finds no emitter at any point in the repository's history** — meaning what depends on them is admin-authored HTML in the database, which is install state and not visible to any scan. *Exit condition:* a migration or a report that counts stored certificate bodies still carrying these classes, reading 0 pending on a real install — the `cpf_rf_encrypted` shape, never a code scan. Logged in #1182; frozen in `CssClassEmissionTest::LEGACY_SHIM`, which is what stops them from being read as dead code again.

**Shim · `assets/img/certificate-defaults/default_background_certificate_3.png` — the background the redrawn model 3 stopped using (#1956).** *Risk if removed:* a form or a user template that still names the file prints with no background, with nothing reporting it — the shipped defaults refresh on reseed, but a form's `_ffc_form_config['bg_image']` and a user template's `_ffc_template_bg_image` copied the URL and are install state. *Why it stays:* #1956 deleted it in the same batch that stopped using it, and no scan can see which installs still point at it. *Exit condition:* a count of forms and pool templates whose background names the file, reading 0 on a real install — the `cpf_rf_encrypted` shape. `CertificateDefaultsShimTest` keeps the file in the tree until then.

**Shim · `SubmissionReader::findForReprint()` — a ticket read by a LIKE over the plaintext `data` (#2241).** *Risk if removed:* on an install without encryption keys no `ticket_hash` is ever written, so a ticket could no longer reprint its certificate, and the spent-ticket check would answer "already used" to the person it was issued to. *Why it stays:* encryption is configured on every install that has the WordPress salts, but nothing in the plugin requires it, and the old lookup ran the scan everywhere. Since #2241 it runs only where `Encryption::is_configured()` is false: with a key every ticket is hashed, and the scan only ever reached rows written before encryption. That narrowing was decided in #2241, and `ReprintLookupParityTest` pins it beside the scenarios where old and new agree. *Exit condition:* encryption becomes a requirement of activation, the way the schema is.

**Shim · `Encryption::try_decrypt()` — the unauthenticated v1 ciphertext read (#2339).** *Risk if removed:* a value written before encrypt-then-MAC (`base64(IV || CT)`, no `v2:` prefix) becomes unreadable — a certificate, an appointment or a profile shows an empty CPF/RF or e-mail, and nothing reports which. *Why it stays:* v1 values can sit in any of the plugin's encrypted columns, options and meta, and the key-rotation migrations re-encrypt only the areas they walk, so no scan can say none remain. *Exit condition:* `Encryption::legacy_v1_reads()` (the `ffc_encryption_v1_reads` option, shown on Settings → Advanced → Encryption Key Health) reads 0 on a real install, or its last read is long past — evidence the old format is no longer read, the `cpf_rf_encrypted` shape. The derivation of the active key from a truncated `FFC_ENCRYPTION_KEY` was weighed in the same pass and deferred by the maintainer: 32 characters are already a strong key, and changing the derivation changes the key every stored value was written with.

_Retired shims and how each was retired — among them the `html/` layout fallback and its directory — are in `docs/engineering/legacy-decisions.md`._

When a new shim is added, log it here (Shim · Location · Risk if removed · Why it stays), and when a new feature makes one unsafe or inadequate, open a specific sub-issue + a breaking-change banner in the CHANGELOG.

### Deprecation cycles — `@removal` is the date, and it fires (#1309)

A shim in the log above is retired by **evidence**; a *deprecation cycle* is retired by a **release**, and that release has to be written somewhere a machine reads. None of the WordPress deprecation functions carries it — `apply_filters_deprecated( $hook, $args, '6.26.0', $replacement )` and `_deprecated_function( __METHOD__, '6.25.0' )` both take the version the thing was **deprecated in**, which is the string WordPress prints to whoever is still listening. The removal release has no field at all, so before #1309 it lived in prose and depended on somebody re-reading the issue at the right moment.

**Write `@removal X.Y.Z` on the surviving code** — a docblock tag on the method or the documented hook, a `// @removal X.Y.Z -- <why>.` line where the thing is a bare registration with no docblock of its own. `DeprecationDueTest` reads it and fails when `FFC_VERSION` reaches that release, naming every site; a second direction refuses any `apply_filters_deprecated()` / `_deprecated_*()` call that carries no marker, which is what stops the first from measuring only what somebody remembered to mark. Deferring a cycle on purpose means **moving the date in the file** — that is the decision, and the code is where it is worth arguing.

**The prose must not restate the number.** The marker is the one place; a sentence saying the same thing is the #1261 class, and one such sentence lives in a *translated* string on the hooks documentation page, which is why that line carries its own marker.

**And prose cannot be the source.** `until 6.24.0` in a docblock is a live promise or a finished story depending on the tense of a verb several clauses away, and no classifier tells those apart reliably. History in the past tense is *correct* and stays; it simply is not a field.

Two mechanics worth not re-deriving. The scan reads **comment tokens**, never raw lines, so a version inside a string literal or a piece of markup can never be mistaken for a marker. And it resolves `T_NAME_FULLY_QUALIFIED` beside `T_STRING`, because `\_deprecated_function(` is one token carrying the backslash — the #1284 trap, pinned here by a canary over synthetic source rather than by what the tree happens to contain.

#### How a shim is retired — evidence or a deprecation cycle

**Retire a shim by evidence when what depends on it is install state; by a deprecation cycle when it is a surface a code scan cannot see** (a public method an external integration might call). Three lessons from retiring the `html/` fallback generalise:

- **Re-measure the surface before retiring a shim.** The inventory records what was known when the shim was logged, not what is true when it is removed; the `html/` removal found twice the sites and one more exit condition than were written down.

- **Keep exit conditions apart that measure different things** — "every install seeds the pool" and "no pending import" are not the same reading, and conflating them nearly retired the shim early.

- **Ship the repair and the removal in different releases**, so an install that needs the repair receives it, and is seen to take it, before it loses the safety net.

The full account is in `docs/engineering/legacy-decisions.md`.

#### Gathering the evidence to remove a **High**-risk shim

Not every High shim is provable by data. Before proposing to build a diagnostic, check whether the evidence already exists:

- **A surface no diagnostic can see is retired by a versioned deprecation cycle**, never by an evidence scan: a public static method with no hook, filter or database trace can have an external consumer nothing reads. Announce it, carry a ⚠ breaking-change banner in the CHANGELOG, and remove it at the second feature release after the notice.
- **Look for evidence that already exists before building a diagnostic.** A migration card's **Pending** count is often the signal already (the `cpf_rf_encrypted` reads went once their migration card read 0 pending on a production install); a parallel counter keyed on the same state is redundant indirection — the façade trap that narrows nothing.

### Parked architecture decisions

- **Import consolidation (recruitment ↔ audience) — parked / not planned (#788).** The #772 export contract deliberately does **not** extend to import: they share only cheap scaffolding, while store, arity and direction diverge, so unifying would be the bad-façade trap. Revisit **only** on a trigger — real audience-import timeouts in production, or a third server-side import duplicating the stage-all→validate→promote shape — then extract from the proven duplication, not on spec.
- **Client-IP default flip (legacy → secure) — parked / not planned (#902, epic #899).** `Core\ClientIpResolver`'s `secure` strategy stays an **admin opt-in** on the IP Diagnostics tab, with a notice recommending it. A forced flip risks collapsing rate-limit and geofence into one bucket on shared hosts, while the non-IP layers (device fingerprint, nonce + capability + per-user rate limit) already carry the load. Revisit **only** on a trigger — concrete evidence of an exploitable IP spoof, or a consumer that genuinely needs the strong signal.
- **Declarative settings registry — parked / not planned (#993).** One `ffc_settings` key is known in up to six places, and a single declaration every consumer derives from would make divergence unrepresentable — at the cost of touching `Settings`, `SettingsReader`, `SettingsSaveHandler`, `SettingsAjaxEndpoint` and many read sites. The cheaper guard is what holds instead: `tests/Unit/SettingsDefaultsTest.php` fails when a read-site default disagrees with the declared one, and its undeclared-key ratchet blocks at zero. Revisit **only** on a trigger — a divergence that cannot be fixed by aligning a literal, or a third consumer of the key list.
- **Vendored runtime bundles vs. Dependabot — parked / not planned (#1208).** Everything Dependabot can see is dev/CI and never ships; everything that ships in `libs/js/` is invisible to it. The decision is the **manual audit**, made cheap by the version in the filename, with `tests/Unit/VendoredBundleInventoryTest.php` freezing the directory so the inventory cannot change without somebody saying so (it cannot see a CVE or verify bytes against upstream). Declaring the bundles in `package.json` only so Dependabot sees them would produce PRs that touch only the lockfile and read as "updated" when nothing was; building them from npm adds the build step the project deliberately lacks and breaks byte-for-byte verification against upstream. Two standing facts: **`ffc-device-signals.js` sets thumbmark's `logging: false`, and that one line is what closes the bundle's remote-`eval` path** (`DeviceSignalsLoggingOffTest` pins it — removing it is a security regression, not a cleanup); and the `html2canvas` handle names the API a third-party script may depend on, while the file and constant carry the maintained fork's name (`html2canvas-pro`). Revisit **only** on a trigger: a published CVE in a bundle, or the next bundle landing in `libs/js/`. The full audit, the thumbmark and html2canvas decisions, and the `qrcodegen` verdict are in `docs/engineering/legacy-decisions.md`.
- **Booking outside the rules on personal calendars — parked / not planned (#1870).** Audience calendars let a bypass holder pick a closed day; personal calendars do not, by decision. Their picker disables closed days for everyone, so the server-side bypass is reachable only for a time-range block inside a working day, and it stays because removing it touches the editor toggle, `ffc_bypass_appointments`, the validator and the role tiers for no present gain. Revisit **only** on a trigger — a real need to book a personal calendar on a closed day, or a change already touching those files (then remove the personal-calendar bypass, with a `CapabilityMigrator` step and a ⚠ CHANGELOG entry if the capability goes).
- **The QR encoder in `libs/phpqrcode/` — kept, not replaced (#2643, #2648).** phpqrcode 1.1.4 is unmaintained, and it stays: it fetches nothing, takes no input but the text, and its output is proved rather than trusted — `QrRoundTripTest` decodes what it draws with chillerlan/php-qrcode (a `require-dev` dependency that never ships) and asserts the exact text at every level. chillerlan/php-qrcode 6 is the replacement if one is ever needed. Revisit **only** on a trigger: a published vulnerability in the encoder, a code the round-trip test cannot read back, or a PHP release that breaks it. `VendoredBundleInventoryTest` freezes the directory's contents.
